Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: The crisis began three years ago when Dat Nguyen’s youngest, Eli, collapsed during a family barbecue. Within minutes, a severe reaction had swollen Eli’s throat, turned his lips a terrifying shade of violet, and forced his chest to hitch in desperate, shallow gasps. Dat had held his son’s trembling hands and watched the blue veins stand out starkly against pale skin as paramedics rushed them to the nearest hospital. That moment etched itself into Dat’s mind. When the evening air grew heavy with darkness, as it does during the long harvest months on his Central Valley property, the familiar hum of the irrigation pumps sometimes harmonized with an old radio station that played those same melodies. The moment Dat caught sight of a neighbor’s child rubbing a swollen ankle, or heard a familiar tune drifting from a pickup truck, the past did not fade into distance; it rushed forward, vivid and suffocating. The specific triggers of visible body parts, nighttime, and certain songs actively pulled the event out of memory and into his immediate awareness, making the hospital room feel as close as his own kitchen. When the sudden sight of a swollen ankle or the drone of a familiar song spiked his panic, Dat found his avoidance strategies kicking in automatically. He delayed sleep, convincing himself he needed to finish equipment repairs, and began avoiding people, turning away from the farm cooperative and stopping phone calls to old friends. Because the memory felt like it was happening right now rather than something that was over, Dat’s fear directly drove him to delay sleep and avoid people. Lying in the dark became impossible; the silence only amplified the phantom beeping of monitors and the imagined sound of his son’s labored breathing. Dat would pace the kitchen until the clock read past two a.m., terrified that closing his eyes would let the reliving event swallow him whole. He told his wife, Meera, that he just needed time to himself, though the exhaustion was relentless. The longer he stayed awake, the more his mind refused to separate then from now. The farm, once a place of steady rhythm, became a landscape of constant vigilance. By isolating himself from neighbors and family, Dat deprived his nervous system of the grounding reassurance that would have softened his reactions. Instead, his sleep deprivation sharpened his threat monitoring, making every creak of the floorboards and every rustle of wind through the cottonwood trees feel like an incoming warning. The longer he avoided human contact, the more potent the triggers grew. When his daily rounds to the south pasture forced him to pass the old community center where evening recitals were held, the local band played a slow, acoustic version of the lullabies that now haunted him. The specific sight of the lead singer’s hands moving over the fretboard triggered a wave of dread so sharp Dat immediately turned his truck around, tires spitting gravel as he fled. The sudden, present-tense memory of Eli’s violet lips would surface during these moments, and that resurfaced memory actively primed his nervous system to fixate on specific body parts and certain songs, sharpening their pull. The avoidance only made the triggers sharper, and when he finally allowed himself to lie down, the darkness would no longer be empty; it would fill with fragments of the event that felt dangerously present, making the prospect of resting feel utterly unbearable. Meera noticed the distance growing between them, his hands trembling around coffee cups, his eyes hollow from nights spent staring at the ceiling. She explained that his survival was slipping away just as fast as his son’s once had, and that nothing would ever be safe if he kept running from the past. Dat finally agreed to schedule an intake, terrified that the memories would one day overwhelm his ability to work the land or hold his family together. He hoped, more than anything, to quiet the noise in his head so he could finally sleep through the night without feeling like he was losing his son all over again.
